analysis.one_liner: Requires farm equipment makers to sell repair parts, tools, software, and manuals to owners and independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to a House committee in September 2023, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that make tractors, combines, and other farm equipment to sell or give owners and independent repair shops the same parts, tools, manuals, and software the companies give their own dealers. It would also let owners get the data their machines generate and unlock electronic security locks so repairs can be done outside the dealer network. The Federal Trade Commission would write the rules and enforce them.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers and ranchers who own or lease equipment, and independent repair shops. Today, when a modern tractor or combine breaks down, owners often cannot fix it themselves or use a local mechanic because the manufacturer restricts diagnostic software, special tools, and parts pairing. The bill would let them repair on their own schedule — critical during planting and harvest windows — often at lower cost. It would also send equipment data back to the owner, and it would place manuals, software, and tools no longer offered even to dealers into the public domain so old machines stay fixable.

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to make repair documentation, parts, embedded software, firmware, and tools available to any equipment owner or independent repair provider on 'fair and reasonable terms' — with documentation free of charge and tools free to farmers.

Bars manufacturers from locking repairs to their dealer network: parts could not be blocked through 'registration, pairing, or approval' requirements, and owners could not be forced to become authorized dealers to fix their own machines.

Lets owners and repair shops bypass electronic security locks and digital rights restrictions specifically to diagnose, maintain, or repair equipment, overriding the copyright law provision that manufacturers otherwise use to stop third-party repairs.
Requires manufacturers to hand over the data a machine generates, either to the owner or to an independent shop with the owner's authorization.
Makes the Federal Trade Commission the enforcer, treating a violation like an unfair or deceptive practice, and directs the agency to write the rules.
Keeps old equipment repairable: when a manufacturer stops offering a part, tool, or documentation even to its dealers, any copyright or patent on it goes into the public domain.

analysis.who_pays: Farm equipment manufacturers — companies like John Deere, CNH, and AGCO — which would lose some of the high-margin service, parts, and software revenue that comes from being the only ones who can fix a machine. The bill tries to soften this by protecting trade secrets (except where needed for repair), leaving authorized-dealer agreements alone, and banning modifications that defeat emissions controls, safety systems, or other laws. Some compliance costs could ultimately show up in equipment prices.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers would lose revenue from being the sole provider of dealer-only repairs, diagnostics, and parts — money that helps fund engineering, and some of the lost margin could be recovered through higher equipment prices for farmers.

Opening security locks and repair software to anyone raises real cybersecurity and tampering concerns, including the risk that modified equipment could evade emissions controls or disable safety warnings; the bill's answer is a list of prohibitions in Section 6 rather than a technical safeguard, and critics would argue enforcement after the fact is not enough.

The FTC would have to write detailed rules for a technical, fast-changing market, and critics of that approach say one-size-fits-all federal rules could mandate disclosure of sensitive design information even with the bill's trade-secret carve-out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete and time-sensitive: a combine that fails mid-harvest can be fixed in hours by a local mechanic instead of waiting days for a dealer's scheduled visit, and repair bills drop when farmers can do the work themselves. The costs are real but limited — the bill was drafted to avoid forcing disclosure of trade secrets, to leave dealer contracts intact, and to ban modifications that break emissions or safety rules. The main design weakness is that it leans on FTC rulemaking and after-the-fact prohibitions to handle security risks rather than building them into the requirements. On balance it transfers bargaining power from manufacturers to equipment owners at a modest, mostly commercial cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and no one ever brought it up again before the term ran out.

narrative.text: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a Democrat from a rural Washington district, introduced the Agricultural Right to Repair Act on September 20, 2023.

The same day, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which holds jurisdiction over the FTC and most right-to-repair proposals; two days later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce.
Nine Democratic colleagues cosponsored the bill, but it received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm equipment manufacturers keep their exclusive control over parts, repair software, and dealer service networks, and the service and parts revenue that comes with it. Farmers gain nothing; they remain dependent on manufacturer dealerships for repairs.

for.name: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited nine cosponsors; represents a rural Washington district where equipment repair access is a live constituent issue.

for.name: Nine House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; all nine were Democrats, and none was a member whose support moved the bill out of committee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Innovation, Data, and Commerce Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from September 2023 until the Congress ended without scheduling a hearing or markup, which under House rules prevented any floor vote.

against.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Led the committee that never took up the bill; no markup was scheduled during her chairmanship.

against.name: Farm equipment manufacturers (John Deere, CNH, AGCO and their trade associations)
against.what_they_did: Fought federal right-to-repair legislation as a group, arguing that unrestricted access to software and repair tools creates safety, emissions, and cybersecurity risks; Deere and farm-equipment dealers pushed a voluntary industry agreement instead.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the record shows only that all 10 supporters (the sponsor plus 9 cosponsors) were Democrats; right-to-repair proposals have drawn some Republican interest, but none here.
